newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan hosts appear to fall out with Saudi exile.
newsitem.headline: Afghan hosts appear to fall out with Saudi exile.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic movement appeared on Wednesday to have fallen out with exiled Saudi Arabian dissident Osama bin Laden, telling him to stop anti-Saudi activities.
Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar personally conveyed the advice to bin Laden during a meeting with him on Tuesday in the southern Afghan city Kandahar, the official Kabul radio said.

The broadcast, monitored in Islamabad, said Omar, whom Taleban regards as the Islamic Amir-ul-Momineen (leader of the faithful), told the wealthy Arab to "stop propaganda and warnings against Saudi Arabia".

Afghan sources in Pakistan said Omar's call was a clear reprimand and the purist Taleban's first public disapproval of the ideas of bin Laden, who has lived in Afghanistan under Taleban protection after being forced out of Sudan under Saudi pressure last year.

Earlier, a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service quoted a Taleban statement from Kandahar as saying Omar told the exile to "have good attitude towards Saudi Arabia as it is the centre of Moslems and hosts Kaaba", Islam's holiest shrine in Mecca.

Bin Laden, a multi-millionaire financier stripped of his Saudi citizenship because of his activities against the royal family, has threatened to wage a holy war on "crusader" U.S. forces in the homeland of Islam.
He has been named by the United States as a prime suspect in two bombings in Saudi Arabia that killed 24 U.S. servicemen and two Indians and wounded more than 400 people in 1995 and 1996.

AIP quoted the Taleban statement as saying Omar told bin Laden in reply to a question that Saudi Arabia had invited the American forces when it felt a threat of invasion from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
But he said the American forces should now leave Saudi and other Arab territories because no further threat existed.
Last Saturday, an official in Yemen denied that bin Laden had gained a foothold there and said his country opposed "terrorism".
The Taleban, which controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, says it will not allow the war-shattered country to be used for activities against any other country.
